issues.legal_issue: A rent-control requirement for prior permission to terminate a tenancy by a landlord does not apply when the tenant chooses to surrender the tenancy.
material_facts: The landlords applied for permission to terminate the tenancy under the applicable rent-control order.
The tenant then agreed to surrender the tenancy rights and undertook to vacate the premises by an agreed date.
The Rent Controller filed the proceedings after the parties submitted their compromise.
issues.conclusion: Prior permission was not required because the tenancy was terminated by the tenant’s surrender, not by the landlord’s determination of the tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13 of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 restricts the landlord’s right to determine a tenancy and requires permission when the landlord seeks to terminate it. It does not restrict a tenant from surrendering the lease. Sections 106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognize termination by either lessor or lessee and the ending of a lease by surrender.

predicates.rent_control_permission_proceeding: A landlord sought permission in a proceeding to terminate a tenant’s lease under a rent-control restriction.
predicates.tenant_agreed_to_surrender: The tenant agreed to end the tenancy by surrendering the tenancy rights.

issues.definition: When a landlord sought permission to terminate a tenancy but the tenant agreed to surrender it, prior permission was not required for that surrender.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s surrender may end a tenancy despite the tenant remaining in possession, and an arrangement for time to vacate and payment for use and occupation after surrender does not continue or create a tenancy.
material_facts: The tenant agreed in a compromise to surrender the tenancy and later signed an arbitration agreement stating that the tenancy rights had been surrendered.
The resulting award and decree allowed the tenant further time in possession in return for damages for use and occupation.
The tenant remained in possession after the agreed surrender, but the later arrangement neither continued the old tenancy nor created a new one.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy ended by mutual agreement and surrender even though possession was not physically handed over; the later arrangement was not a contract to evade the rent-control restriction, and the decree based on it could be executed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 111(e) and (f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease may end by express or implied surrender. In Shah Mathuradas Maganlal & Co. v. Nagappa Shankarappa Malaga, AIR 1976 SC 1565, the Court explained that surrender may be inferred from mutual consent and related conduct. Foster v. Robinson, [1950] 2 All E.R. 342, supports the conclusion that continued physical possession does not prevent a finding of surrender where the parties’ arrangement determines the old tenancy. An arrangement fixing time to vacate and damages for occupation after surrender does not itself continue or create a tenancy.

rule.if: eviction_decree_execution_proceeding and parties_mutually_agreed_to_end_tenancy and post_surrender_arrangement_only_allowed_time_to_vacate and tenant_remained_in_possession

predicates.eviction_decree_execution_proceeding: A party sought execution of a decree for possession based on the ending of a tenancy.
predicates.parties_mutually_agreed_to_end_tenancy: The landlord and tenant mutually agreed that the tenancy would end.
predicates.post_surrender_arrangement_only_allowed_: After agreeing to end the tenancy, the parties arranged for the tenant to remain temporarily while paying for use and occupation until vacating.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_possession: The tenant did not physically hand over possession when the tenancy was agreed to end.

issues.definition: When parties mutually ended a tenancy, a later arrangement only allowed time to vacate, and the tenant remained in possession, the surrender could still be effective.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor who had an opportunity to challenge a decree but did not do so may be barred from raising that objection later in execution proceedings.
material_facts: The tenant received notice when the arbitration award was placed before the court and did not object that the decree could not be passed without rent-controller permission.
The tenant also did not raise that objection during an earlier execution proceeding, despite opportunities to do so.
The tenant first raised the objection in a later execution proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from raising the objection belatedly, and constructive res judicata applies in execution proceedings; the Court considered this an additional ground, though its decision on surrender made it unnecessary to rely on it.
issues.legal_principle: The principles of constructive res judicata apply in execution proceedings. Mohanlal Goenka v. Benoy Kishna Mukherjee, AIR 1953 SC 65, applied those principles to execution proceedings. An objection available when a decree is made, but not raised despite an opportunity to do so, may not be raised later in execution.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to execute a court decree.
predicates.objection_available_before_decree_was_pa: The judgment-debtor could have raised the objection when the award or proposed decree was before the court.
predicates.judgment_debtor_did_not_raise_objection_: The judgment-debtor received an opportunity to raise the objection but did not do so.
predicates.objection_first_raised_in_later_executio: The judgment-debtor first raised the objection in a later execution proceeding.

issues.definition: When an objection could have been raised before a decree was passed but was not raised despite an opportunity, raising it for the first time in a later execution proceeding is barred.
